summary: How to get the built AAPS APK onto the phone and install it (via Google Drive or a USB cable), what the Play Protect warning means, and how Google's Android developer verification (from September 2026) affects installing self-built apps, with four free ways to keep installing AAPS: ADB, the web installer, the advanced flow and a limited distribution account. Bold and quoted labels are Android system, Google Drive and Play Protect labels, not app strings.

sections.heading: Transferring and Installing AAPS on your smartphone
sections.summary: Page title and intro: transfer the APK to the phone, install it, and read about the upcoming developer verification.

sections.heading: Installing AAPS by tapping the APK file
sections.summary: Installing by opening the APK on the phone, the two transfer options, and a warning that developer verification may block this.

sections.heading: Option 1. Use Google drive to transfer files
sections.summary: Uploading the APK to Google Drive from a computer.

sections.heading: Use the Google Drive app to execute the apk file for installation
sections.summary: Opening the APK in the Google Drive app on the phone, temporarily allowing installs from Drive in Android settings, then revoking it.

sections.heading: Option 2. Use a USB cable to transfer files
sections.summary: Copying the APK to the phone's Downloads folder by cable, allowing installs from that source in Android settings, installing, and disabling the permission again.

sections.heading: Google Play Protect warning
sections.summary: Play Protect's unsafe-app warning is expected for a self-built app; tap through to install anyway.

sections.heading: Android developer verification
sections.summary: Introduces Google's requirement that installed apps come from a verified developer, including sideloaded APKs.

sections.heading: What is changing
sections.summary: How the check works at install and update time, and the rollout timeline by country.

sections.heading: Does this affect me?
sections.summary: Who is affected and when: building and running AAPS are unaffected; installs and updates may be blocked depending on country and date.

sections.heading: Free ways to install AAPS
sections.summary: Choosing among the four free installation methods depending on whether a computer is available.

sections.heading: Option 1: Install with ADB (computer needed)
sections.summary: Enabling Android developer options and USB debugging, then installing or updating AAPS from a computer with adb install -r.

sections.heading: Option 2: Install from a web page (computer, no command line)
sections.summary: Using the AAPS web installer page in Chrome, Edge or Opera over USB debugging, also from a second Android phone.

sections.heading: Option 3: The "advanced flow" on your phone (no computer needed)
sections.summary: Turning on Android's Allow apps from unverified developers in developer options, the 24-hour waiting period, and choosing to allow indefinitely.

sections.heading: Option 4: Register with Google (free limited distribution account)
sections.summary: The free limited distribution developer account and why its use with AAPS is still untested.

sections.heading: What does not change
sections.summary: Building, GitHub and keystores, the installed app with its settings and objectives, and ADB installs are unaffected.

sections.heading: Where to get help
sections.summary: Where to read Google's FAQ and ask the community, and what details to include.
